turns.zh: 另一个让我着迷的例子是特斯拉。特斯拉的使命宣言是：“加速全球向可持续能源转型。” 他们甚至不强调自己是汽车公司。特斯拉不会说：“我们比福特和丰田更优越。” 这点至关重要，因为伟大的运动往往诉诸更高的目标。它们不会说：“我比X公司更出色。我是安飞士，服务更贴心。”而是描绘一个更具美学吸引力的未来愿景。然后证明这家初创公司正是实现这一愿景的载体，这也为接下来讲故事提供了绝佳契机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One other quick example I'm thinking about linear is kind of pushing this movement of craft and design and experience matters in B2B software. And you shouldn't settle for something that you don't love.
turns.zh: 我还能想到另一个快速案例：Line正推动B2B软件领域的工艺、设计和体验至上运动。人们不应满足于不爱用的产品。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Very much so. And you know what, Chesky, I don't think he even knew he was fully doing this at the time, but Chesky did this brilliantly with Airbnb. So he created a movement around living like a local. And so the other thing that a movement does is it turns the greatest strength of the status quo into its biggest weakness. And so Brian never said, "Hotels suck. Death to the Four Season." He just said, "Hey, look, when you go to Paris, you have a choice. You can hang out in the Four Seasons and it's going to be just like the Four Seasons everywhere else in the world. It'll be in the middle of the town, or you can live in Paris like a Parisian." And he's like, "I don't have to say that the Four Seasons is bad for you to decide to choose me. And oh, by the way, if you want to stay in the same kind of hotel everywhere you go, I'm not for you." (01:11:31): But so now let's say you're four seasons, your whole business is predicated on doing a good job of having a common experience that people could accept and that they're used to and that they expect. And so now you've taken all of the stuff that you invested decades in and turned it into something you have to apologize for all of a sudden. And so the great startups, they create movements not so much by criticizing the incumbent, but by showing the weakness in the strength of the incumbent. And then just saying to the customer, "Hey, look, you decide it's not up to me to decide what's bad about Four Seasons. It's up to you to decide whether you value my difference or not."
turns.zh: 确实如此。说实话，切斯基，我觉得他当时甚至都没意识到自己在这么做，但他在Airbnb上把这件事做得非常出色。所以他开创了一场关于"像当地人一样生活"的运动。而运动的另一个作用是，将现状的最大优势转化为其最大的弱点。布莱恩从不说“酒店很烂，四季酒店万岁”，他只是说：“嘿，听着，当你去巴黎时，你可以选择住在四季酒店，那里和世界其他地方的四季酒店一模一样。它位于市中心，或者你也可以像巴黎人一样生活在巴黎。”他说：“我没必要说四季酒店有多糟糕，你自然就会选择我。顺便说一句，如果你想去哪儿都住一样的酒店，那我就不适合你。”（01:11:31）但现在假设你是四季酒店，你的整个业务都依赖于提供一种人们能够接受、习惯且期待的标准化体验。现在你却把自己投入数十年的成果，突然间变成了需要为之道歉的东西。优秀的初创公司创建运动，不太在于批评现有企业，而是揭示现有企业优势中的弱点，然后对客户说：“嘿，听着，是否要批评四季酒店的坏处，这不该由我来决定，而是由你来决定你是否看重我的与众不同之处。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of counter positioning from Hamilton Helmer's Seven Powers book.
turns.zh: 这让我想起汉密尔顿·赫尔默在《七种力量》一书中提到的反向定位策略。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: A hundred percent.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So to make it even more practical for people that are like, "Oh, I need to come up with a movement for my startup. That's why things aren't working." It sounds like it's kind of here's how we want the future to look and why we're doing this. And then it's a combination of marketing, positioning, messaging, repeating it, social media, imagine is that roughly how to think about?
turns.zh: 所以对于那些说“哦，我需要为我的初创公司想出一个运动策略，否则事情就无法推进”的人来说，要让它更具实用性。听起来就像是这样：我们希望未来是什么样子，以及我们为什么要这样做。然后再结合市场营销、定位、信息传递、不断重复、社交媒体、想象力，大致就是这么个思路吧？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: But I would also say that it's about storytelling. And so storytelling, there is a science to storytelling. And so for example, the hero's journey, you have somebody in the world that is the hero, let's say Luke Skywalker on Tatooine, dusty planet, he's bored out of his mind. And then a mentor shows up and offers them a call to adventure, Obi-Wan Kenobi. And at first they resist the call, but then something bad happens in this case, Luke's like, "Hey, I can't come with you. I got chores to do for Aunt Beru and Uncle Owen." But then he comes back to his place and it's all burned down the storm troopers killed his aunt and uncle. So then he accepts the call. The mentor has a tool and a magic. In this case, it was the lightsaber was the tool and the magic was the force. (01:13:32): And they need those things because the hero has to have a reason to credibly believe that they can beat the bad guy. And so then what happens is you find co-conspirators along the way, Han Solo, Chewy, ultimately the princess. You rescue her, you blow up the death star, you beat the empire, and then emerge, transform. They even get medals at the end of the movie, right? Now, it turns out that the exact same thing applies for startups. So if we take the Lyft example, let's just say I'm a rider. In the past, the world that is taxi suck in [inaudible 01:14:10]. I can't even get one. And when I get one, it's gross and it smells bad and it's late, and they won't take my credit cards. I have to have cash. They can't rely on them to get me there. I guess my alternatives to park, you can't ever get parking people break into your car. That's the world that is. (01:14:28): Logan and John would engage in a call to adventure, "Try this ride-sharing app. It shows cars on map, you know where they're all the time, they come within five minutes, fist bumped the driver." Now, this was where the genius of the pink mustache came in. So the pink mustache honored the fact that a lot of times people resist the call. It's scary to get into stranger's car. So the pink mustache made it seem a little bit less scary. When you see these cars driving around in San Francisco, you're like, "Hmm, what's up with that pink mustache?" And you're talking to your friend and they say, "Oh, it's this new thing called Lyft. It's pretty cool. It's an app if you've seen it." And so Logan and John did, among the best I've ever seen at honoring the fact that people might resist the call. (01:15:13): But then part of the story is languaging. This was the genius of Twitter. They didn't call it Microblogs, Inc., right? They created a metaphor around tweeting birds. The Tesla was this way, right? It wouldn't have survived a comparison with a Porsche of 9/11. The seats weren't as good, the radio wasn't as good, but Elon was telling a story about a different future. And when you bought the Tesla Roadster, you weren't buying it for practical reasons. You were buying it for aesthetic reasons. You were buying it because you thought that that future was something you wanted to be part of. So the storytelling primitive ends up working spectacularly well for startups, right? We need to describe the world that is, we need to describe the world that could be, which is that different future. We need to understand, and this is important that your job as the founder is to be Obi-Wan, not Luke. (01:16:04): So the founders sometimes make the mistake of thinking that they're the hero, but they're not. The early believers are the heroes, and it's the job of the founder to tell a story that emotes early believers to want to move with them and co-create the future with them. And the story you tell an employee is different from the story you tell an investor is different from the story you tell a customer because all of them have a different idea of what their hero's journey. If you're an investor, maybe your idea of being a hero is to make a hundred times your money and be on some fancy list and make money for your LPs. If you're an early customer, maybe you're a hero by solving an important business problem and getting recognized for it in your company. If you're an early employee, maybe it's you want to work on something you're excited about with really awesome people that don't waste your time with politics and bureaucracy, all of those are different journeys. All of those are different transformational ways to self-actualize. And we have to meet those people where they are and give them a reason to want to come with us to the world to be.
turns.zh:
然而，我还要说，这关乎讲故事的艺术。讲故事其实是一门科学。比如"英雄之旅"模式：故事中会有一个身处平凡世界的主人公，比如《星球大战》里的卢克·天行者。他在塔图因星球上无聊至极，直到奥比-万·克诺比出现，召唤他踏上冒险之旅。起初卢克抗拒这个召唤，但当坏事发生时——比如暴风兵杀害了他的叔婶——他最终接受了使命。导师手中掌握着工具与魔法（本例中是光剑与原力），而英雄必须有可信的理由相信自己能击败反派。随后他会结识同伴（如汉·索罗、丘伊），拯救公主，炸毁死星，最终战胜帝国并蜕变。影片结尾他们甚至获得勋章，对吧？  

同样的逻辑也适用于初创企业。以Lyft为例，假设我是一名乘客。过去打车体验糟糕透顶：等不到车，司机态度恶劣，迟到又不收信用卡，还得付现金。停车更是不靠谱，车被撬走……这就是现状。  

洛根和约翰用"试试这个拼车应用"的创意抓住了核心：地图显示车辆位置、实时追踪、五分钟内到达、司机握手致意……粉色胡子设计更是妙招。它巧妙化解了用户对陌生人拼车的恐惧——当你在旧金山看到粉色胡子时，会好奇"这是什么梗"，朋友解释后你会感兴趣。  

还有特斯拉的营销：不叫"微博客公司"，而是用推特鸟的比喻；特斯拉路斯特的定位不是比拼性能，而是讲述未来愿景。消费者购买特斯拉，不是因为实用，而是因为认同其未来理念。  

讲故事的本质对初创企业同样适用：描述现状，勾勒愿景。创始人必须像奥比-万一样充当导师，而非主角。早期信徒才是真正的英雄，创始者的任务是用故事激发他们的共鸣。
与他们同行，与他们共创未来。你向员工讲述的故事，与向投资者讲述的故事不同；向客户讲述的故事，又与向投资者讲述的故事不同，因为他们对英雄之旅的理解各不相同。若你是投资者，或许你心目中的英雄形象是赚取百倍收益、跻身权威榜单、为有限合伙人创造价值；若你是早期客户，或许你通过解决重大商业难题成为英雄，并因此在公司获得认可；若你是早期员工，或许你渴望与志同道合的伙伴共同攻克激动人心的挑战，不必为办公室政治和官僚主义浪费精力。所有这些都是截然不同的旅程，都是实现自我价值的不同蜕变之路。我们必须在他们所处的阶段与他们相遇，为他们提供一个愿意与我们共创世界的理由。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had Nancy Duarte on the podcast. She is one of the most famous presentation designers, and she had exactly the same advice. When you're trying to tell a story, you basically bounce back between the world that is, the world that could be. What is, what could be. What is, what could be, and just keep going back and forth.
turns.zh: 我在播客中邀请了南希·杜阿尔特。她是全球最著名的演示设计师之一，而她的建议如出一辙。当你试图讲述一个故事时，本质上就是在世界现状与理想未来之间来回切换——现状如何？未来可能如何？如此反复。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: A hundred percent. In fact, Nancy is the person who helped me understand this better than any single person. So Nancy would show me how Steve Jobs's iPhone launch speech. She'd be like, "Okay, well now notice what he does. He shows how bad phone suck now. They have styluses, they have keyboards." And then he talks about what could be, you could combine an internet communicator, you could combine an iPod, and he goes back and forth between how bad the current state of things is, how it should be, how bad it is, how it should be. Introducing the iPhone, how bad it was, how awesome it's going to be, how awesome it is. When you look at his speech, he's masterful at toggling. And by the way, the same is true. Abe Lincoln with the Gettysburg Address, "Four score and seven years ago, new nation, now we're in a civil war. We need to preserve what we stand for as a country. We need to go win this war." But he kind of goes back and forth drawing a tension between what has happened in the world that was, and the world that could be.
turns.zh: 完全赞同！事实上，南希是唯一一个比任何人都更让我深刻理解这一点的人。比如她会向我展示史蒂夫·乔布斯发布iPhone时的演讲片段。她会说：“好的，现在注意他的做法。他展示了现有手机有多糟糕——有触笔、键盘。”接着他会谈论未来可能：你可以把互联网通讯器和iPod结合起来。他在现状与理想之间反复切换——现状多糟糕，理想又如何。介绍iPhone时，他先说现状有多糟糕，再说未来会多棒，最后又强调现状有多棒。看看他的演讲，他在这种切换上堪称大师级操作。顺便说一句，亚伯拉罕·林肯的《葛底斯堡演说》也是如此：“147年前，一个新生国家如今深陷内战。我们要守护国家精神支柱，赢得这场战争。” 他也在现状与理想之间反复切换，勾勒出历史与未来的张力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that I was thinking as you were talking was, I've seen too many founders spend so much time crafting this amazing story and vision of their product, and they have this really cool blog post and big idea, but nobody really cares about their product yet. Do you have any advice of just make sure you're building something people want above all else. And the story is a layer on top of that.
turns.zh: 听你讲时我一直在想：太多创业者花大量时间精心构思产品故事和愿景，写出超酷的博文和宏大构想，但产品还没得到用户认可。你有没有建议，要确保首先打造出人们真正需要的东西？故事只是锦上添花。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: So many startups I see the first slide is like, "We're Acme AI software. We're located in San Francisco, we're funded by X and Y VCs." That's not storytelling because you're talking about yourself, right? And if you're trying to make the person in the audience the hero, they don't care about you yet. They care about how you're going to make them a hero. And so when you kind of say, 'Okay, if I'm pitching VCs, what I really need to do is help them understand why they'll be a hero if they invest in my company according to what makes them feel heroic." What you present is different, but what a lot of startup presentations do is they take their sales pitch and they rehost it for every other audience. They rehost it for the press, for investors and for employees and all that. And that's wrong because what you're doing is you're talking about yourself to different people, but what you want to do is describe the world that could be, the stakes that are involved, and then each of those individual audiences, you want to meet them where they live in the world that is, and show them how they can engage in a transformational journey to the world it could be.
turns.zh: 我见过太多初创公司，首页幻灯片都是：“我们是Acme人工智能软件，总部位于旧金山，由X和Y风投支持。” 这根本不是讲故事，因为你在自我介绍，对吧？如果你想让听众成为主角，他们现在对你是谁不感兴趣，他们想知道你如何让他们成为英雄。所以当你说：“好吧，如果我在向风投推销，关键在于让他们明白投资我们公司能如何成就英雄。” 你的演讲内容有所不同，但很多初创公司会把销售推销文本照搬到不同受众面前。比如向媒体、投资者、员工等重复讲解。这是错误的，因为你在向不同群体讲述自己，但你真正要做的是描述理想未来，阐明面临的挑战，然后根据每个受众的现状，找到他们身处的世界，并向他们展示如何踏上通往理想未来的变革之旅。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also share your amazing stats and backgrounds and market size and all that stuff.
turns.zh: 还要分享你的惊人数据、背景、市场规模等信息。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Yeah. Although it's funny, I've found that investors are the same. Investors, ultimately they believe or they don't believe. A lot of times, this is the other thing I see happen, is the poor founder will get advice from 20 different people about their pitch deck. And a lot of the people giving them advice are not believers in that different future. They're giving generic startup advice or they'll go pitch a bunch of firms and they didn't consider who's prepared to possibly believe, who isn't. And so then they get objections to their pitch from people who aren't going to believe anyway, and then they try to have a slide to meet that objection. And before you know it, you have what I call a Franken deck. And so you have this huge, gigantic presentation trying to anticipate every objection, and the person who was ready to believe you in the first place doesn't know what you were trying to say because you obscured it with all this other stuff. And so I find that just like with an insight, it's okay if most investors don't like your idea, what you want to find is the ones who are prepared to move with you and make sure they absolutely know why they should. To me, that's the ideal pitch deck.
turns.zh: 是啊。虽然这听起来挺有趣的，但我发现投资者都一个样。说到底，投资者要么相信你，要么不相信你。我还经常遇到这样的情况：创业者会就他们的PPT演示文稿征求20个不同人的意见。然而很多给他们建议的人，并不相信他们所描绘的未来。他们要么给出千篇一律的创业建议，要么四处推销却不考虑哪些投资者真正愿意相信他们的愿景。结果，他们得到的反馈都是来自那些根本不买账的人，然后又试图用幻灯片来回应这些反对意见。不知不觉间，他们就拼凑出了一个所谓的“拼凑版PPT”。最终，他们打造了一个庞大的演示文稿，试图预先应对所有可能的质疑，但最初愿意相信你的人却因为被过多冗余内容蒙蔽了双眼而搞不清你的核心主张。所以我发现，这就跟创意洞察一样。大多数投资者不喜欢你的想法没关系，你要找到那些愿意与你同行、并深切理解其价值的人。在我看来，这才是理想的PPT演示文稿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this advice. And just to be clear, this is like seed and pre-seed before there's a lot of traction, a lot of data and like that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个建议了。再说清楚一点，这是在种子轮和天使轮阶段，还没有大量数据和市场验证的时候。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Exactly, exactly.
turns.zh: 没错，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what's your advice to a founder that's trying to iterate on their deck is it's just like, "Don't show it to too many people." Is it, "Stick to your guns."
turns.zh: 那么对于正在优化PPT的创业者，你的建议是什么？是"别给太多人看"，还是"坚持自己的信念"？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Okay, here would be my succinct advice. And other than that, there's about a million details. Slide one, you say what you do as if I literally know nothing. So it's not, "We're Airbnb, we're a marketplace for unused residential housing space." Bad. But you'll get advice that says to do that because VCs think marketplaces are hot, residential real estate's big. What you should instead say is something like, "We're Airbnb, we let you rent an extra room in your house." Because now as the VC, I'm like, ah, I know what you do. And there are a lot of pitches, I'm 10, 15 minutes in and I'm trying to understand what they do, but I don't know. So you just say, "Here's what we do." (01:22:26): And then the second thing that I say to people is, I think your second slide ought to be, here's the thing we know that's not obvious. So when I was raising fund one for Floodgate, I would go to an LP and say, "We believe that there's a gap between Angels and VCs. VCs are writing $5 million checks. Angels $250,000 checks. We believe that 500,000 is the new 5 million because of Lean Startups. We believe that there will be a new type of category funds called seed funds. Now, if you don't believe that, nothing else I'm about to say is going to make any sense to you, I can just give you your time back." [inaudible 01:23:06]. But then once, if they did believe that or they were in a position to lean forward, now when they start mentioning my competitors, I say, "Okay, well, recall Peter Fenton works at Benchmark, he's not going to compete with me because why would Peter Fenton leave Benchmark to start Seed Fund doesn't make sense. The only people who are going to try to compete with me from the big funds are the people who aren't performing." (01:23:26): But if you set the context of what your insight is, you can always come back to it. When they bring up competitors, you can always come back to it when they bring up objections and you can say, "Hey, remember I'm just telling you we need to agree on this insight for this to have a chance of being great." So what do we do? What's our insight? And then slide three is what, if any, proof points do we have? We have any customers? Do we have great founders? Is there something happened already that should cause you to believe that my insight is vowed?
turns.zh:
好的，我会给出简洁的建议。除此之外，还有无数细节。第一张幻灯片，你把自己做的事描述得好像我对此一无所知。比如：“我们是Airbnb，是未被充分利用的住宅空间交易平台。” 这不对。但有些人会建议你这么做，因为风投认为市场平台很热门，住宅房地产领域规模巨大。你应该改成：“我们是Airbnb，让你可以出租自家多余的房间。” 这样一来，作为风投的我就能明白你们在做什么了。很多推介会上，听了10到15分钟后，我还在试图理解他们的业务，但始终不得要领。所以你只需要说：“这就是我们做的。” （01:22:26）  
第二点建议是，你的第二张幻灯片应该讲清楚一个显而易见却常被忽视的真相。比如，我为Floodgate筹集第一轮资金时，会对LP说：“我们认为天使投资人和风投之间存在巨大鸿沟。风投写500万美元的支票，天使投资人写25万美元的支票。我们相信，由于精益创业，50万美元将成为新的500万美元标准。我们认为种子基金将成为新型的投资类别。” 如果对方不认同这一点，我接下来说的任何话都毫无意义，我会直接结束对话。（01:23:06）  
但一旦他们认同了这一观点，或者愿意进一步探讨时，我会提到竞争对手：“好吧，请记住Peter Fenton在Benchmark工作，他不会和我竞争，因为Peter Fenton离开Benchmark去创办种子基金根本说不通。只有业绩不佳的风投才会试图与我竞争。” （01:23:26）  
通过设定你的洞察力背景，你可以随时回归主题。当他们提及竞争对手时，你可以回归；当他们提出异议时，你可以说：“嘿，记得我说过我们需要达成共识，否则这项业务很难成功。” 那么我们该怎么做？我们的洞察力是什么？第三张幻灯片是我们有哪些证明点？我们有客户吗？我们有优秀的创始人吗？是否已经有某些事件发生，让你相信我的洞察力是正确的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. I love this tangent we went on...
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。我喜欢我们延伸出的这个话题……

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: ... site is out.
turns.zh: ……网站上线了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love this. I love this tangent we went on. Let me come back to the actions that you found the most successful startups end up taking. We've talked about movements, we've talked about storytelling. The third is my favorite, I'm excited to hear you talk about it, which is disagreeableness. What is that about?
turns.zh: 太喜欢这个了。我喜欢我们延伸出的这个话题。让我再回到你认为最成功的初创公司采取的行动上。我们讨论了行动力，我们讨论了讲故事。第三个是我最喜欢的，很期待听你谈论它，那就是“不合群”。这是什么意思？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Earlier, I'd mentioned that you want to escape the comparison trap when you have your insight and when you have your idea, in creating movements and telling stories, you want to break free from the conformity trap. We always are under pressure to conform in this world, and people use the pressure of conformity to prevent us from exploring things outside of our limits. There's a book that I love called Jonathan Livingston Seagull, where there's a seagull who wants to fly at infinite speed, and all the other seagulls are like, "Look, we're just destined to eat crap off the surface of the ocean. That's just what we are. We're seagulls." He ends up getting banished from the flock because everybody thinks he's crazy. To me, the great founders are kind of like Jonathan Livingston Seagull. They're willing to pursue something that they're obsessed with, that they think has to happen in this world, and they're willing to sacrifice their status in the socioeconomic sometimes dominance hierarchy because fulfilling the mission is ultimately more important to them than fitting in. (01:25:31): You can't stand out if you always fit in. The only people who are different can really make a difference. That's kind of the mindset. I like to say a startup is a fundamentally disagreeable act in the first place, and there's going to be times you need to be disagreeable. I've seen this time and again. I hear people say to me, "I want to work with a founder who's coachable." I'm like, "I'm not really sure." Sometimes I used to joke that when I would meet with Ev Williams, my whole job was to give him advice that he ignored. I would say to him, "Hey, Ev. I don't think you should raise that much money, because I think you'll spend whatever you raise in 18 months, no matter how much you raise." He said, "Man, so you mean that startups almost always spend their money in 18 months regardless of the amount?" I said, "Yeah. I call it Mike's Law. It almost always happens, because once you have the money, all the pressure is on you to spend it." (01:26:26): He is like, "Man, that is a really good advice. I'd never thought of it that way before. That sounds right to me." Well, he proceeds to go raise a shitload of money, but he did stuff that I didn't think he should do, but it worked. I liked that in him. A lot of people would say, "Well, doesn't it bother you that he didn't listen to you that much?" No, because he was disagreeable, and he was the right kind of disagreeable. He didn't say, "Pound the sand. I'm not listening to you. La-la-la, I'm covering my ears." He listened and he understood what I thought the truth was. He just believed a different truth than I did, and that's fine. My job as the investor is to just help them see what my perception of the truth is, honestly. If they decide to go in a different direction, that's great. They're the founder, they're the genius. (01:27:22): All of them, not all of them, but a whole lot of them are more disagreeable than history lets on. My dad worked for Bill Gates when he was at Microsoft. Bill Gates is not a warm and fuzzy dude. He was tough. He was a hard ass. But great people are inspired by hard asses, as long as the hard ass makes ... You meld the steel in the heat of the flame of high standards. Sometimes people can't work for Elon Musk for very long, but almost everybody I know who's worked for him really respects him, because he has high standards, and he's not trying to win friends and influence people. He's trying to land on Mars, and if you're going to land on Mars, you got to be disagreeable some of the time. I just find that that is a trait that is under-appreciated in these great founders quite often.
turns.zh:
早些时候，我提到过，当你有了自己的洞察力和想法时，你要摆脱比较陷阱。在创造运动和讲述故事时，你要突破从众陷阱。在这个世界上，我们总是承受着从众的压力，而人们利用这种压力来阻止我们探索超出自身界限的事物。我很喜欢《海鸥乔纳森》这本书，书中有一只海鸥想以无限的速度飞翔，而其他海鸥却说：“看，我们注定只能吃海面上的垃圾。这就是我们的命运，我们是海鸥。”最终它被驱逐出了群体，因为人们认为它疯了。对我来说，伟大的创业者就像乔纳森·利文斯顿海鸥。他们愿意追寻自己痴迷的事物，认为这些事物必须在世间发生，甚至愿意为此牺牲自己在社会经济层级中的地位，因为完成使命对他们而言比融入群体更为重要。（01:25:31）：如果你总是随大流，就无法脱颖而出。只有与众不同的人才能真正有所作为。这就是创业者的思维模式。我常说创业本质上就是一种与众不同的行为，有时你必须敢于反抗。我多次见证过这种现象。有人对我说：“我想和一个愿意接受指导的创始人合作。”我说：“我不太确定。”有时我开玩笑说，每次和埃文·威廉姆斯会面时，我的全部工作就是给他那些被他忽视的建议。我对他说：“埃文，我觉得你不该融资那么多钱，因为无论你融资多少，18个月内都会花光。”他说：“天哪，你是说创业公司无论融资多少，18个月内都会把钱花光？”我说：“是的。我称之为‘迈克定律’。这几乎每次都会发生，因为一旦你有了钱，就必须把钱花出去。”（01:26:26）：他说：“天哪，这建议真棒。我以前从未这样想过。这听起来很合理。”接着他去融资了一大笔钱，但做了一些我认为不该做的事，但结果却奏效了。我欣赏他这一点。很多人会说：“他不听你的话，你难道不生气吗？”不，因为他敢于反抗，而且是恰当的反抗。他不会说：“闭嘴，我不听你的。啦啦啦，我捂住耳朵。”他会倾听，理解我的观点。只是他相信的真理与我不同，这没关系。作为投资者，我的职责就是诚实地帮助他们看清我眼中的真相。如果他们决定另辟蹊径，那也很好。这是他们的创始权，他们是天才。（01:27:22）：他们中的许多人——不是全部，但很多——比历史所展现的更有反抗精神。我父亲曾在微软为比尔·盖茨工作过。比尔·盖茨可不是个温和友善的人。他很强硬，要求严格。但伟大的人会被这种严格所激励，只要这种严格能……在高标准的烈焰中熔炼钢铁。有时人们无法长时间为埃隆·马斯克工作，但我认识的几乎所有为他工作过的人都非常敬重他，因为他标准极高，而且他不是在讨好别人，拉拢人心。他在登陆火星，而要登陆火星，就必须敢于反抗。
时间。我只是觉得，在这些伟大创始人身上，这种特质往往被低估了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What you just shared reminds me of a recent podcast episode of Jeffrey Pfeffer, which I know you listened to, where he talks about the rules of power, how people acquire power, and the last rule is, "Understand that once you have acquired power, what you did to get it will be forgiven, forgotten, or both." Your Bill Gates example, I think, is a good one where people look at him as such a nice dude when, as you said, he was not so nice a lot of the time.
turns.zh: 你刚刚分享的内容让我想起杰弗里·普费弗（Jeffrey Pfeffer）最近的一期播客节目，我知道你也听过。他在节目中谈到了权力的规则、人们如何获取权力，最后一条规则是：“要明白，一旦你获得了权力，你获取权力的手段将被原谅、遗忘，或两者兼有。” 我认为比尔·盖茨（Bill Gates）的例子很典型——人们把他视为一个好人，但正如你所说，他很多时候并非如此。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Here's the other thing, and by the way, I listened to that episode from beginning to the end, and I thought it was fantastic, because the next thing I want to do is go to Professor Pfeffer and say, "Can we cast these seven principles through a pattern breaking lens?" Let's assume you're a startup capitalist, you're not at a company, because changing the future requires you to acquire a different form of power than you would, say, in an organization. But as I was listening to it, I was like, "These principles all apply to pattern breakers, all of them, every single one." The other one is that I think that he said, "Not everybody's going to like you. If you want to be liked, get a dog. But if you want power, there's certain things you're going to have to do and reconcile yourself with." (01:29:36): Acquisition of power has this notion of you've got to wield the carrot and the stick. If all you do is wield the carrot, you won't create enough activation energy for people to move to that different future. Sometimes you do have to use the stick, and sometimes you have to realize that people are going to use your desire to fit in against you. They're going to say, "Oh, you can't do that. That's illegal," or, "You can't do that, that's unethical," or, "You can't do that. You're being some tech bro, bad guy." A lot of what I find with the founders I work with, ironically, before they win, they have to have the courage to be disliked because people don't like their idea. They think it's stupid, lonely. (01:30:20): But then after they win, it's even worse, because everybody says you cheated or you're a bad guy or you broke the rules or you're too powerful, or, "Who gave you the right to decide what the future should be?" They get criticized unfairly in the other direction after they succeed, but in the end, it comes with the territory. It's part of the job description, unfortunately.
turns.zh: 还有一点，顺便说一下，我从头到尾听完了那期节目，觉得非常棒，因为接下来我想做的是去找普费弗教授问：“我们能否用打破常规的视角来解读这七条原则？” 假设你是一位创业资本家，不在公司任职，因为改变未来需要你获取与在组织中截然不同的权力形式。但听节目时，我一直在想：“这些原则全都适用于打破常规的人，每一条都适用。” 另一条原则是，他说的“不是每个人都会喜欢你。如果你想被喜欢，就养条狗。但如果你想要权力，就必须做出某些决定，并与自己和解。” （01:29:36）：获取权力有这样一个概念——你必须运用胡萝卜加大棒的手段。如果你只用胡萝卜，就无法为人们创造足够的行动能量去迈向那个不同的未来。有时你必须动用大棒，有时你必须意识到，人们会利用你渴望融入的欲望来反对你。他们会说：“哦，你不能这么做。这是非法的。” 或者，“你不能这么做。这不道德。” 或者，“你不能这么做。你就是个自以为是的科技狂人，坏家伙。” 讽刺的是，我发现和我合作的创始人们，在成功之前必须有被讨厌的勇气，因为人们不喜欢他们的想法。他们觉得这很愚蠢、很孤独。（01:30:20）：但成功之后，情况更糟了，因为每个人都说你作弊了，或者你是个坏人，或者你违反了规则，或者你太强大了。或者，“谁给了你决定未来的权利？” 成功后，他们会受到不公正的批评，但说到底，这就是这份工作的本质。不幸的是，这是工作描述的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Elon goes through a lot of that. Something I saw you tweet recently along these same lines is that most successful companies, there's tons of chaos internally, and everyone working at these companies is like, "This place a mess. How is this even working?" But your finding is that that's very common and normal.
turns.zh: 是啊。埃隆（Elon）也经历了很多类似的事情。我最近看到你发的推文也提到了同样的观点：大多数成功的公司内部都充满混乱，每个在这些公司工作的人都会说：“这个地方一团糟。它怎么还能运转下去？” 但你的发现是，这非常常见、非常正常。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Especially in startups. There have been times when I've said things like, "Execution doesn't matter," and people can misinterpret that. When I mean execution doesn't matter, I don't mean people shouldn't get things done or people shouldn't say, "What did you do this week?" But when I think of execution in a corporate sense, corporations in theory should always win. They have big management team, they have more experienced people, they have customers, suppliers, partners, brand, so a startup never beats a big company by executing better than the big company. Startup wins over the big company because it proposes a radically different future, disorients the incumbent, and sort of chaotically moves people to that different future. (01:31:46): But like every startup I've ever seen, on the inside was wild. It was like a capitalist mutation. It was trying to find a beaked finch in the Galapagos Islands that's never been discovered before, and it's all ambiguous all the time, and people are arguing about what the right direction is all the time. It's just messy, but movements are messy. That's what comes with the territory. A friend of mine, Robin Roberts, once said, "Make your mess your message." It's so true.
turns.zh: 尤其是在初创公司里。有时我会说"执行并不重要"之类的话，但人们可能会误解我的意思。当我说执行不重要时，我并不是说人们不该把事情做好，或者不该问"你这周做了什么？"而是从企业层面来理解执行时，理论上大公司应该总是更胜一筹。它们拥有庞大的管理团队、更丰富的经验、客户、供应商、合作伙伴和品牌，所以初创公司永远无法通过比大公司更出色的执行来击败它们。初创公司之所以能战胜大公司，是因为它们提出了一个截然不同的未来，让现有企业感到困惑，并以一种混乱的方式将人们引向那个不同的未来。（01:31:46）但正如我见过的每一家初创公司内部一样，一切都乱成一团。这就像一场资本主义突变。就好比在加拉帕戈斯群岛寻找从未被发现的喙嘴雀，整个过程充满不确定性，人们总是在争论正确的方向是什么。这种混乱是必然的，但正是这种混乱造就了机会。我的朋友罗宾·罗伯茨曾说过："让你的混乱成为你的讯息。"这句话太对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. That's so funny. I love it. I have a couple more questions before we wrap up. Before we leave the actions categories, is there anything else you think is important to share, any other lessons that we haven't touched on?
turns.zh: 天哪，太有意思了。我太喜欢了。在结束之前，我还有几个问题。回到行动类别，你觉得还有什么重要的东西值得分享，或者还有哪些我们尚未触及的经验教训？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: I think, Lenny, I don't know if you've consciously tried to do this or not, but on some level you've created a movement. No one has ever engaged people with product management sensibilities the way you have. I go to your site, and you even have merch for product managers. I'm like, "What?" I imagine the early posts that you wrote, it probably felt kind of lonely. It's probably, "I wonder if anybody's even reading this stuff," but it starts to accumulate. More people start to read it, more people start to tell their friends about it, and now all of a sudden, it kind of becomes a thing. In many ways, Lenny's podcast and Lenny's blog and Lenny's newsletter are all examples of facets of this movement that you're creating. (01:33:26): But your movement is not just about the stories you tell or the guests you have or the podcasts or the write-ups you have. You have a point of view about the centrality of a product manager in companies and in businesses and in the future, and honoring that the way Nike honors athletes. The point of view is the movement, just like the point of view is the company when it's a startup. This point of view is the story. It's the place that people want to go that got animated by the beliefs that you share.
turns.zh:
莱尼，我不知道你是否有意识地这样做过，但在某种程度上，你已经创造了一场运动。没有人像你这样以产品管理的思维方式吸引人们参与其中。我访问你的网站，甚至还有为产品经理设计的周边商品。我当时就想："什么？"我能想象你最初写的那些帖子，可能感觉很孤单，心里在想："不知道有没有人读这些内容。"但后来关注度逐渐增加。越来越多的人开始阅读你的内容，告诉他们的朋友，现在突然间，这就成了一个热潮。在很多方面，莱尼的播客、博客和通讯都是你正在创建的这场运动的不同侧面。
（01:33:26）但你的运动不只是关于你讲述的故事、邀请的嘉宾、制作的播客或撰写的文章。你对产品经理在公司、商业和未来中的核心地位持有一种观点，正如耐克对运动员的尊重一样。这种观点就是这场运动，正如在初创公司中，这种观点就是公司本身。这观点就是故事。这是人们想要去的地方，而这个地方因你所分享的信念而充满生机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating and flattered. I have no intention of starting a movement. I could see what you're saying. That sounds like a lot of stress, but I guess-
turns.zh: 太有意思了，也受宠若惊了。我无意发起一场运动。不过我能理解你的意思。这听起来压力很大，但我想——

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: I think you already have, whether you met to or not, I think you have.
turns.zh: 我觉得你已经做到了，无论你是否承认，我认为你已经做到了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Well, I do have swag, and if you're on YouTube, this is our best-selling item, a hat that just says "Product Manager." People love it. I have it in the background. [inaudible 01:34:26]
turns.zh: 好吧。我确实有周边商品，如果你用YouTube的话，这是我们最畅销的商品，一顶写着"产品经理"的帽子。人们很喜欢它。我把它放在了背景里。[01:34:26不可听清]

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Can I wear one if I'm still not one?
turns.zh: 如果我还不是产品经理，我能戴一顶吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. You've been one, and so forever product manager. I'll send you a hat.
turns.zh: 绝对的。你曾是这样的人，所以永远都是产品经理。我会给你送顶帽子。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Hopefully, I can get grandfathered in for my past.
turns.zh: 希望我能凭借过往经历获得特殊待遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Forever. Forever PM Mike. Okay. I just have one more question, and this is around your last chapter, which I think is going to be useful to a lot of people. Your last chapter is about how to apply a lot of these principles to working at a company. Say you're not a founder, a lot of these principles still apply. What advice can you share for people, say, a PM, instead of large company to help them find pattern-breaking ideas, big ideas within the company?
turns.zh: 永远。永远做产品经理迈克。好的，我还有最后一个问题，关于你的最后一章，我认为这对很多人都会有用的。你的最后一章讲的是如何将许多这些原则应用于公司工作。假设你不是创始人，很多这些原则仍然适用。对于像产品经理这样的人，从大公司跳槽到小公司，帮助他们在公司内找到突破常规的想法、大创意，你能给出什么建议？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: The first thing I think is important to understand is that everything about a value delivery system when you're doing a pattern-breaking idea is different from a normal idea. The mistake that most companies make is they say, "I've got this new pattern-breaking idea. It needs to be a third of my business in 24 months or three years or whatever." Bad strategy. Let's take a company like, say, Apple, when they did the iPhone. The iPhone was a whole new thing. It was driven by, in this case, Steve Jobs the founder. You couldn't reconcile it with the original business of the Mac and not really even the iPod. You had to treat it as a totally different thing, and that's really hard for companies. Companies make the mistake of engaging in a pattern-breaking product, but they make it too visible or it's a career-limiting move if it fails. Pattern-breaking products have different types of leadership, different types of go-to-market motion as we've described, different types of ideas, different risk profiles. Instead of saying this company or this business is too big to fail, I need to make small bets that can fail a lot. The same is true with mergers and acquisitions. If I buy a company, I need to ask, am I buying a pattern-breaking company to break the pattern of my business and go in a radically new direction, or am I buying a company that's an extension of my current business? Neither is wrong per se, but the way you think about risk varies enormously. (01:36:43): Some examples that I have in the book of good examples are the iPhone, Steve Jobs, AWS, but some people objected. They said, "Okay, that's easy for the founders to do because they're founders of the company, and that's Steve Jobs and Jeff Bezos." The other example I like is Skunkworks with Lockheed. When they created a fighter plane in a very short amount of time, and that's how they did it, they had an organization totally separate from the main organization, somebody with absolute power, and tried to make it not visible, tried to make it be separate. Because when you make it visible, you start to drift it back into the tractor beam of acting like a pattern-matching corporation. Another good example back in the day was Don Estridge at IBM when they did the IBM PC, but it's almost always an autonomous business headed by a maverick, and you're trying to do something discreetly different rather than a better version of what you've already.
turns.zh: 我认为首先要理解的是，当你进行突破性创新的想法时，价值交付系统的方方面面都与普通想法不同。大多数公司犯的错误是，他们会说：“我有了一个新的突破性想法。它需要在24个月或三年内占据我业务的三分之一。”这是一个糟糕的策略。以苹果公司为例，当他们推出iPhone时，iPhone是一个全新的事物。在这种情况下，它是由创始人史蒂夫·乔布斯推动的。你无法将它与Mac的原有业务，甚至iPod的业务相协调。你必须将它视为一个完全不同的事物，而这对公司来说非常困难。公司会犯一个错误，即参与突破性产品，但又让它太显眼，或者如果失败了，这会成为职业发展的障碍。突破性产品需要不同的领导方式、不同的市场推广策略、不同的创意类型、不同的风险概况。与其说这家公司或这项业务太大而不能失败，不如说我需要进行小规模的尝试，这些尝试可能会失败。并购也是如此。如果我收购一家公司，我需要问自己，我是在收购一家突破性公司，以打破我业务的常规模式，走向一个全新的方向，还是我在收购一家扩展我当前业务的公司？两者本身并没有错，但你对风险的看法截然不同。（01:36:43）：我书中提到的一些好的例子有iPhone、史蒂夫·乔布斯、AWS，但有些人反驳道。他们说：“好吧，这对创始人来说很容易做到，因为他们是公司的创始人，那是史蒂夫·乔布斯和杰夫·贝索斯。”我喜欢的另一个例子是洛克希德的Skunkworks项目。当他们在很短的时间内制造出一架战斗机时，他们就是这样做的。他们有一个与主组织完全分离的组织，有一个拥有绝对权力的人，并试图让它不被外界注意，试图让它保持独立。因为当你让它变得可见时，你就会开始让它回到与常规公司相一致的轨道上。另一个早期的好例子是IBM的唐·埃斯特里奇，他们推出了IBM PC，但它几乎总是由一个特立独行的创业者领导的自主业务，你试图做一些谨慎的不同之处，而不是对现有事物的改进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This aligns very well with, we had two recent podcast episodes talking to PMs at companies that are doing zero-to-one stuff, Mihika and Tanguy. Tanguy had a really interesting tidbit along the lines you just talked about where he set up his team in a totally different time zone so that people that wanted to bug them just were sleeping during that time, and they weren't even online so that they could just focus on the work they were doing, and it worked out.
turns.zh: 这与我们最近的两期播客非常契合，嘉宾是来自那些正在进行“从零到一”创新的公司的产品经理——米希卡（Mihika）和坦古伊（Tanguy）。坦古伊分享了一个很有趣的案例：他把团队安排在不同时区，这样那些想找他们麻烦的人只能在休息时间联系他们，而团队成员根本不上线，这样就能专心工作，最终取得了成效。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: I'm mostly through that episode, and everything that I've listened to so far, I'm like, "Okay, that totally jives with what I've seen." The other person has an interesting take on this is Vinod Kochblok. Vinod basically thinks that what companies should do is take some portion of their profits, let's say 10% of your profits, and invest it in projects likely to fail, but with wildly asymmetric upside if they succeed, and then make them not visible to the mothership in the early inning. It's your willingness to fail that lets you have breakthrough success. (01:38:49): Any coin that says can't lose bad on one side of it might as well say, can't win big on the other side. It's your willingness to fail, and it comes back to departing from the consensus, right? It's your willingness to fail that enables success, and every time you depart from the consensus, there's a chance you'll be wrong, you'll underperform the consensus, but it's your willingness to do that that lets you outperform it. But there's no shortcuts, right? The coin that says can't lose, says can't win on the other side, and lose big says, win big on the other side.
turns.zh: 我基本听完了那期节目，到目前为止所听到的内容都让我感同身受。另一位对此有独特见解的是维诺德·科赫布洛克（Vinod Kochblok）。维诺德认为公司应该拿出部分利润，比如10%，投资那些可能失败但一旦成功则会带来巨大回报的项目，并且在初期阶段不让总部知晓。正是愿意承受失败的勇气，才让他们能取得突破性成功。（01:38:49）：任何硬币的两面都是非赢即输。你愿意承受失败，就意味着你也愿意承受巨大的风险。但正是这种愿意承受风险的态度，才让成功成为可能。每次偏离共识，都有可能出错、表现不佳，但正是这种敢于偏离共识的勇气，才让他们能超越共识。然而没有捷径可走，对吧？硬币的一面写着“不能输”，就意味着另一面写着“不能赢”，而“输大”则意味着“赢大”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mike, this episode is so full of nuggets, tactical advice, amazing stories, everything I was hoping it would be. Before we get to our very exciting lightening round, is there anything else that you think might be useful to share with folks that are trying to start a company or are already along with a company?
turns.zh: 迈克，这期节目真是干货满满，充满了实用建议和精彩故事，完全符合我的期待。在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你是否还有其他建议，可以分享给那些正尝试创办公司或已经在经营公司的听众？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Yeah. The one thing I would say is that it's a lonely existence, and it's okay if most people don't like your idea. It doesn't mean you're right, but it sure as heck doesn't mean you're wrong either. There's not enough people in this world willing to stick their neck out for things that they believe that they see before the rest of us. Just for what it's worth, if anybody in your audience is one of those people, you have just my utmost respect and affection. I hope that in those times when it's tempting to not believe, it comes with the territory every great founder has faced, and it doesn't make you wrong.
turns.zh: 是的。我要说的是，创业之路注定孤独。如果大多数人不喜欢你的想法，这没关系。这并不意味着你一定正确，但也绝不意味着你错了。这个世界上愿意为自己所信仰、比其他人更早看到的事物挺身而出的人太少了。说真的，如果听众中有这样的人，我对你们充满敬意和感激。我希望在那些令人怀疑自己的时候——每个伟大创始人都曾面临的考验——你们能坚持下去，这并不会让你们错了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. What an empowering, inspiring way to end it. Mike, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。多么振奋人心、鼓舞人心的结尾啊。迈克，接下来我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Okay, here we go.
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Here we go. First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始。第一个问题，请推荐两到三本你最常向他人推荐的书籍？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: A book called The Five Regrets of the Dying, Top Five Regrets of the Dying by Bronnie Ware. She was a hospice nurse, and she would talk to people in the last 90 days of their lives, and she would find out the things that they'd wish that they had done in their lives that they hadn't. I always thought that that was a good book, because it reminds you about what's important, and it reminds you that it isn't going to last forever. Someday, it'll be the last day. (01:41:20): There's another book that I really like called Chase, Chance, and Creativity by a guy named James Austin, and I think that it's a good book because it talks about how certain people tend to attract luck more than others and actually that luck is created, you do make luck. I am just fascinated by this idea of luck and how it can be harnessed. I'd say those two. There's a whole bunch of them. I've always liked all of Clay Christensen's books. The other one that I kind of liked that I read recently is by Robert Greene, The Laws of Human Nature. I liked that one a lot as well. Then Nancy Duarte's book, Resonate, we talked about Nancy earlier, I like that book a lot.
turns.zh:
有一本叫《临终者的五大遗憾》的书，作者是临终关怀护士布罗妮·韦尔。她会与生命最后90天的人交谈，发现人们最遗憾自己未曾做过的事。我一直觉得这本书很棒，因为它提醒你什么才是重要的，同时也让你意识到生命不会永恒，总有一天会走到尽头。

（01:41:20）还有一本我很喜欢的书，叫《追逐、机遇与创造力》，作者是詹姆斯·奥斯汀。我觉得这本书很棒，因为它探讨了为何有些人比其他人更容易吸引好运，而好运其实是可以创造的，你自己就能创造好运。我对这种关于运气及其可控性的观点很着迷。就选这两本吧。书单上还有很多，我一直很喜欢克莱·克里斯滕森的所有书籍。最近读的罗伯特·格林的《人性法则》也让我印象深刻。还有南希·杜阿尔特的《共鸣》，我们之前提到过这本书，我也很喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm buying that first one immediately. That sounds incredible. I need that book. Regrets of the Dying. I found it on Amazon as you were talking, and I'm buying it. Good pick there. Okay, next question. Is there a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 我马上就买第一本。听起来太棒了。我需要这本书。《临终者的五大遗憾》。我在你说话的时候就在亚马逊上找到了这本书，马上就买了。选得真不错。好的，下一个问题。你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: I really liked the movie about Enzo Ferrari, and I have this huge affinity for 1960s cars, and the way that they replicated these 1960s Ferraris I just thought was magical. I thought that the guys that did the special effects and just the attention to detail I thought was just extraordinary.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢关于恩佐·法拉利的电影，我对60年代的汽车有着深厚的感情，他们复刻的60年代法拉利车型简直太神奇了。那些特效团队和对细节的关注简直令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have not seen it. Quick aside, as I was buying this book, your book was recommended on Amazon for me, so good job.
turns.zh: 我还没看过。不过顺便说一句，我买这本书的时候，亚马逊还推荐了你的书，干得好。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Oh, good. Okay. Here we go.
turns.zh: 太好了。好的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good job, Amazon. I will point people to where to find it at the end of this series of questions, but next question, is there a favorite product that you have recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 亚马逊真棒。我会在问答结束时告诉大家哪里能找到这本书，但下一个问题，你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: When I was young, before I got into computers, I had a job as a professional calligrapher, and so I really like using calligraphy pens. Not long ago I sort of discovered the world, it had been a long time since I'd reconnected with that hobby, I discovered the world of vintage fountain pens. My favorite product of recent times, everybody will be like that sounds esoteric, but it's a Mont Blanc 149 first generation celluloid pen. It was right after World War II, and it was the Germans coming back saying, "We've still got it." It was just a product for the ages. It has a flexible nib. Fountain pens don't work the way they used to. They used make flexible nibs so that you could write the way scribes wrote in the 1800s and stuff. But then people in the modern world break those nibs, and they use ballpoint pens anyway. But when I use these old flexible pens from 1900 to the 1940s, they're just magical. There's just nothing like it. Nobody's ever been able to equal that experience in modern times.
turns.zh: 我年轻时，在接触电脑之前，做过专业书法师，所以我很喜欢用书法笔。不久前我重新发现了这个爱好——复古钢笔的世界。最近最喜欢的产品？大家可能会觉得这听起来很冷门，但是一支万宝龙149一代赛璐珞笔。它诞生于二战后，德国人战后回国时说：“我们还有这些东西。”这是一款永不过时的产品。它配有灵活的笔尖。现在钢笔的使用方式和过去不同了，人们用球形笔尖来模仿19世纪的书法笔尖。但当我使用这些1900到1940年代的灵活笔尖时，那种体验简直不可比拟。现代再也没有能比得上的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I got to try one of these pens.
turns.zh: 哇。我得试试这种笔。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Yeah. I'll give you one of them so you can at least get a feel for it.
turns.zh: 是啊。我会给你一支，让你至少能感受一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I'll give you a product management hat, I'll get a pen, a beautiful pen. I think I win in this exchange. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often repeat to yourself, share with folks that you find useful to come back to?
turns.zh: 哇。我要送你一顶产品经理帽，再拿一支漂亮的笔。我觉得这次交流我赢了。还有两个问题：你有没有最喜欢的的人生格言，经常默念，或者觉得很有用，值得反复回味的？

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: I learned it from my dad. It sounds simple, but it's kind of profound, "Do your best." What he meant by that is he didn't mean be the best, he meant that life is a gift. You don't know how much time you're going to have. Every day is the gift of your time, and the best way to honor the gift of your time is to do your best. There'll be times you won't be the best, but if all you did was the best, that's all you could do. I remember one time, so I was a senior in high school, I'd already gotten into Stanford, I'm totally psyched, I'm going to go. Last week of the semester of senior year, and I have a test the next day in English. (01:45:29): My dad's like, "Hey, how are you feeling about the test?" I said, "It doesn't really matter. I get to drop it, and I'm going to get an A in the class, because I've got the goods, so I don't need to do well on it." He looked so disappointed at me, and he was like, "It doesn't sound like you're doing your best." What he was kind of getting at was that the people who achieve greatness, they think everything counts. I always got a lot from that with him. There'd be other times where I wouldn't do so well on something, and he would say, "Well, sometimes you make a careless mistake, but you did your best. That's all you could have done." (01:46:15): The idea of doing your best I find to be very profound, and it causes you to realize that the best way to show up in the world is to be your best self. There's only one you in this world, and the more that you can show up as your best self, you'll be impossible to compete with, you won't feel the need to copy other folks, you won't feel the need to compare yourself to other people. You'll compare yourself instead to the idea of perfection itself and whatever that means in terms of your own ability to do your best. To me, that's probably the most important life lesson I've learned.
turns.zh: 这是我从我父亲那里学到的。听起来很简单，但其实很有深意——“尽你最大的努力”。他这么说的意思不是要成为最优秀的人，而是说生命是一份礼物。你不知道自己还有多少时间。每一天都是上天赐予的礼物，而尊重这份礼物的最好方式，就是尽自己最大的努力。当然有时候你做不到最好，但只要尽了全力，也就无憾了。记得我高三那年，已经被斯坦福录取了，超级兴奋，正准备去读。高三最后一周，第二天要考英语。（01:45:29）我爸问：“你对这次考试感觉如何？”我说：“无所谓，反正能拿A，因为我水平在那儿。”他听了特别失望，说：“这听起来你根本没尽全力。”他想说的是，那些能成就大事的人，都认为每一件事都很重要。我从他那里收获了很多。还有其他时候，我做得不好， 他会说：“有时候你会犯粗心的错误，但你已经尽力了。这就是你能做到的最好了。” （01:46:15）尽力而为这个理念对我来说非常深刻，它让你意识到，展现自我的最佳方式，就是成为最好的自己。在这个世界上，你只有一个人，当你尽力展现最好的自己时，别人就无法与你竞争，你也不必模仿别人，更无需与他人比较。你只需与自己的最佳水平比较，以及自己尽力做到最好的能力。对我来说，这大概是我学到的最重要的人生经验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. As you said, very simple but very powerful.
turns.zh: 哇，正如你所说，简单却非常有力量。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: It's powerful when you truly internalize it, right? When you take it beyond an aphorism, it's very powerful.
turns.zh: 当你真正领会它的深意时，它才有力量，对吧？当你把它从一句格言提升到更高的层次时，它就非常有力量了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of your partner, Anne Marie Coe's advice that she got from her dad, which is I think maybe the opposite that she shared on Tim Ferris' podcast of just always do a world-class job at everything you do. You're doing a world-class job.
turns.zh: 这让我想起了你的搭档安妮·玛丽·科伊从她父亲那里得到的建议，我觉得可能和她在蒂姆·费里斯播客上分享的观点相反，就是无论做什么都要做到世界级水准。而你现在就已经在做到了。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, I'm going to skip the last question just to end on that, because that was way too beautiful to Sully with another question. Just to give folks a chance to figure out where to buy your book, when it's available, how to find it, what they should know, do share.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我跳过最后一个问题，就到这儿吧，因为再问下去就太扫兴了。给大家一个机会，了解一下你的书在哪里买，什么时候上市，如何找到它，需要知道什么，真的很值得分享。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: I guess there's two main ways, right? Well, we've got a Substack. Not everybody's got to buy books, right, so there's patternbreakers.substack.com. Then I have a site, patternbreakers.com, but you can also get the book on Amazon or anywhere. It's already available for pre-order, I think.
turns.zh: 我猜主要有两种方式，对吧？首先，我们有 Substack。不是每个人都需要买书，对吧？所以有不走寻常路的人。substack.com。然后我还有一个网站，patternbreakers.com，但你也可以在亚马逊或其他平台购买。我觉得现在已经可以预购了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I usually ask people how listeners can be useful to you. I imagine it's check out the book, share what you've learned.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我通常会问听众如何能为你带来帮助。我想应该就是去看看这本书，分享你所学到的知识。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: My main goal is for the ideas to spread and to help people. Hopefully, it will have achieved that goal. But just anything that people can do to help spread the ideas. Co-conspirators wanted.
turns.zh: 我的主要目标是让这些理念得以传播并帮助到人们。希望我们已经达成了这个目标。但只要大家能为传播这些理念出一份力就好。欢迎志同道合者加入。

turns.en: I love these episodes where somebody like you spends hundreds of thousands of hours analyzing data and history and startups and talking to founders and just synthesizing all the things you've learned into a couple of hours. I love this. Thank you, Mike, so much for being here and for sharing all this wisdom with us.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这样的节目——像你这样的人会花数十万小时分析数据、研究历史、研究初创公司、与创始人交流，然后把所学的知识浓缩成几个小时的分享。我太爱这个环节了。非常感谢你，Mike，感谢你今天的到来，与我们分享这些智慧。

turns.speaker: Mike Maples, Jr.
turns.en: Hey. Well, thanks, Lenny. It was an honor to be on your show, and it's been fun to see you do so well.
turns.zh: 嘿。嗯，谢谢你，Lenny。很荣幸能参加你的节目，看到你事业如此成功真是太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks, Mike. It's an honor to have you on the show. Again, the book is called Pattern Breakers: Why Some Start-Ups Change the Future. Mike, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Mike。很荣幸你能来参加节目。再次强调，这本书叫《破局者：为何有些初创公司能改变未来》。Mike，非常感谢你的到来。

turns.en: Okay. See you, Lenny. Thanks.
